description: This team requires a self built project with interactive blowing stories of the abandoned spacebots.
summary:
Postcards from Silent Explorers is a storytelling project created for the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten.” It is a slideshow prototype in which four NASA Mars robots (Sojourner, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity), none of them still operating, each write a first-person postcard back to Earth. Every postcard describes where the robot landed, what it discovered and how its mission ended, followed by quick facts and a quiz. An answer key at the end lets students check their answers.

The project addresses the challenge by turning retired NASA equipment into stories instead of leftover hardware. Each robot has its own voice and personality: Sojourner the tiny trailblazer, Opportunity the marathon runner, InSight the listener and Ingenuity the explorer of the Martian sky. Research was also done on Moon equipment, including Surveyor 1, Surveyor 3 and the Apollo rovers, but because the creator learned about the challenge only one day before the hackathon began, these could not be added. With limited time, a Canva slideshow was built instead of a full website.

The project is important because these robots made major discoveries, from ancient water to a liquid core inside Mars to the first powered flight on another planet, yet many students have never heard of them. Storytelling makes the facts easier to remember and can spark curiosity about space. Facts come from NASA and JPL pages, and the AI assistant Claude helped draft the text and cross-check numbers.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
My project is called Postcards from Silent Explorers, and I made it by myself. It gives a voice to four NASA Mars robots that aren’t working anymore: Sojourner, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity. Each robot “writes” a postcard back to Earth in its own voice, telling you where it landed, what it discovered and how its mission ended. Every postcard has quick facts and a small quiz, and an answer key at the end lets students check themselves.

What are the benefits?
Students learn real NASA history in a fun way instead of just reading dry numbers. The first-person voice makes dates and distances easier to remember, and the quizzes let them test themselves. A teacher could use one postcard as a quick class starter or all four as a full lesson.

What is the intended impact?
I picked this idea because of the challenge name, “Abandoned but not Forgotten.” These robots are still on Mars where their missions ended, and I think their stories deserve to be remembered. I want students to feel curious about space and science. Sojourner was the first rover on Mars and proved that a small rover could work there. Opportunity found signs of ancient water and set the off-world driving record. InSight listened to marsquakes and showed that Mars has a liquid core. Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet and flew more than 14 times farther than NASA planned.

What tools did I use?
I designed the slides in Canva. My facts came from NASA and JPL pages (science.nasa.gov, jpl.nasa.gov, nasa.gov), and my pictures came from the NASA Image and Video Library. I used an AI assistant, Claude, to help me search those pages, pull out key facts, and draft the postcard text and quiz questions. I didn’t write code or use special hardware.

How is it creative?
Instead of a table or a timeline, each robot has its own personality: Sojourner is the tiny trailblazer, Opportunity the marathon runner, InSight the listener and Ingenuity the explorer of the Martian sky. The postcard format and quiz turn a mission report into a story.

What did I research and consider?
I cross-checked every number against NASA pages and fixed my mistakes, like InSight’s exact count of 1,319 marsquakes, calling InSight a lander and not a rover, and Sojourner’s weight of 10.6 kg. I also learned that Pathfinder’s airbag landing system was used again for later rovers, that Opportunity was the first rover to identify sedimentary rocks on another planet, and that InSight was the first mission since Apollo to focus on seismology beyond Earth. I also researched Moon equipment for the “Moon and Mars” part of the challenge. NASA’s Surveyor 1 made America’s first soft landing on the Moon in 1966 and sent back more than 11,000 TV images. Surveyor 3 dug trenches in the soil, and in 1969 Apollo 12 landed about 155 meters from it and the astronauts took home its camera. NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has photographed the Apollo sites and can even see the lunar rover parked where it was left. I also thought about my audience (middle and high school students), about giving credit to NASA, about telling the truth about my AI use, and about calling the robots “retired” and not “trash.”

What are the limits of my project?
Sadly, I couldn’t add the Moon robots because I only found out about this challenge one day before the hackathon began. Since I worked alone with very little time, I made a slideshow prototype in Canva instead of a full website.

What would I do next?
With more time, I’d build an interactive website where you flip each postcard and answer the quiz with instant feedback. Then I’d add Surveyor 1, Surveyor 3 and the Apollo rovers, more Mars robots, and other languages so more students can use it.

Where the new research comes from (so you can check it)

  • JPL says Pathfinder’s airbag landing system and petal design have been used since to land other rovers on Mars. nasa
  • NASA says Opportunity was the first rover to identify and characterize sedimentary rocks on another planet. nasa
  • InSight’s principal investigator for the seismometer said seismology was the focus of a mission beyond Earth for the first time since the Apollo missions. earthsky
  • NASA says Ingenuity flew more than 14 times farther than planned. nasa
  • Apollo 12 set down on the edge of Surveyor Crater, about 155 m from the deactivated Surveyor 3 spacecraft. im-ldi
  • NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed the Apollo 17 site, where the lunar rover tracks are clearly visible and the rover remains parked east of the lander. nasa
  • Surveyor 1’s 11,000+ images are from NASA Science: science.nasa.gov/mission/lunar-rangers-and-surveyors/
dataRefs: NASA JPL: How InSight Revealed the Heart of Mars
